webTitle: More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican

fields.headline: More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican
fields.trailText: Latest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024
fields.bodyText: More voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to the latest quarterly data published by Gallup. Some 49% of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican. That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president, according to the New York Times. The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash. Trump’s approval rating stood at 52% at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times. But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times. Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democrats reasons to feel optimistic. A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voters surveyed by Gallup identified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.

webTitle: Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military

fields.headline: Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military
fields.trailText: The US defense secretary faces internal dissent and discord at the Pentagon, accused of focusing on culture war issues and his own political ambitions as the Iran war drags on
fields.bodyText: In a different Washington, under a different president, a return to the well-worn playbook of all-out sanctions to counter Iran might have been the signal for a publicity-hungry US secretary of defense to adopt a lower profile. But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary. Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy. The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more. Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East. While the Pentagon insists that any suggestion the defense department is in disarray under Hegseth is “completely baseless”, alarm over his conduct in the role – and the implications – has not merely been expressed by Hegseth’s political opponents. “The secretary of defense is a clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US national guard – in which Hegseth also served – and member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former military leaders. “He has done more harm to the national security of the United States than any secretary of defense since the country was created.” Thom Tillis, the Republican senator from North Carolina, who is stepping down from the US Senate after clashes with Donald Trump, bluntly urged the US president this week to fire his defense secretary. “I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote on social media. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.” After a month-long lull, the resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the strait of Hormuz meanwhile renewed questions over just what the US wants to achieve in its war with the Islamic regime, which Trump and his defense secretary once loudly vowed to topple. The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party. Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation. The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East, where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year. The extensions were ordered even after several commanders in other sectors voiced objections, formally known as “non-concurs”, to the deployments, arguing that they could leave the US at risk of being unable to meet its commitments in other areas, while subjecting forces to the additional strain of being at sea for too long. The non-concurs were recorded in the Secretary of Defense Orders Book of 14 August, a classified document whose contents were leaked and reported by the Washington Post. The Pentagon reached out to the Guardian after publication of this story. Hegseth “has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength”, press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in a statement. “Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all time highs. “Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way. The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.” ‘The past six months has failed’ “I’m not sure what the strategy is here,” Kevin Carroll, a former army colonel and military intelligence officer who served in the offices of the defense secretary and joint chiefs of staff, said of the war on Iran. “What’s the enemy’s center of gravity that we’re going after? “We tried decapitating their leadership. That didn’t work. We tried going after their missile program. We were not able to destroy it. Tried sinking the navy, but they still maintain a mining capability. “We could easily take out their energy infrastructure. But that would drive the price of oil much, much higher, and lead to retaliatory attacks on the energy infrastructure of our Gulf allies. It’s not clear what this target set is intended to do.” Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former White House and state department adviser on Iran, said Hegseth’s long-term deployment orders reflected the administration’s decision to embrace a policy of long-term economic blockade. “It’s a recognition of the fact that the past six months has failed, but they don’t know what to do,” argued Swanson, who suggested that Trump was attracted by the idea of abandoning the conflict, but wanted to do so in way that enabled him to project strength. As the war drags on, Hegseth stands accused of being insufficiently engaged with such grave policy matters, preferring instead to focus on “cultural” issues – sacrificing the careers of talented career officers in the process – and his future political ambitions. The defense secretary, who has evaded awkward questions or scrutiny by not holding a formal Pentagon briefing since 5 May, has reportedly told associates that he is considering a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. In the midst of a burgeoning trade war between the US and Canada, Hegseth – who has previously railed against “fat” generals and instituted testosterone tests for service personnel – found time to wade in by apparently “body shaming” two Canadian female teenage cadets. The social media post attracted a storm of criticism. In a podcast, Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat, accused Hegseth of “fucking online harassment” and denounced the defense secretary as a “punk”. Tensions over Hegseth’s priorities reached a head this week when the army secretary, Dan Driscoll – a friend and ally of Vice-President JD Vance – resigned after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over blocked promotions and purges of senior commanders on flimsy pretexts. A large proportion of those blocked or fired have been black or female, in line with Hegseth’s vocal crusade against “woke” DEI (diversity, equity and inclusiveness) initiatives. In the latest of a series of purges, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had blocked the promotions of seven officers to the two-star general rank. In submitting his resignation, Driscoll – who has spearheaded efforts to modernize the army, including through embracing drone warfare – voiced concerns “surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible”, a source told CNN. Driscoll’s departure – and the reasons for it – aroused anger even among Republicans, most notably Tillis, the outgoing GOP senator. “Dan was the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” wrote Tillis. The withering verdict is seconded by some retired generals, who say misgivings over Hegseth’s leadership are quietly shared by many serving officers who remain. Manner said Hegseth was depriving other parts of the armed forces to fund the Iran war out of “readiness accounts”. “These are for training the rest of the force,” he said. “So the rest of the force is losing training hours, equipment and money for maintenance and operations. The rest of the military is significantly degraded.” Manner also said his conversations with serving officers bore out the leaked concerns voiced in the Secretary of Defence’s Orders Book. “I have firsthand knowledge of people who are serving on active duty who echo the exact same concerns that we are headed to a situation where we can no longer defend Taiwan, that we are very unlikely to be able to defend even, quite frankly, South Korea,” he said. ‘Infinitely worse’ than Rumsfeld Hegseth, who has drawn accusations of war crimes for ordering a succession of strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats off the coasts of South America, is not the first US defense secretary to come under a harsh spotlight over the conduct of a far-off American war. Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Lyndon Johnson, became a lightning rod for criticism during the Vietnam war before eventually undergoing a crisis of conscience and being moved to a new role as head of the World Bank. During George W Bush’s administration, Donald Rumsfeld became the target of fierce criticism after failing as defense secretary to plan adequately for the occupation of Iraq after the initial invasion to topple Saddam Hussein. But Paul Eaton, a retired major general who trained Iraqi troops after the invasion and is now an adviser to VoteVets – an advocacy group for progressive military veterans – said Rumsfeld’s failings paled in comparison with Hegseth. “Rumsfeld had ‘next war-itis’, which was a contributing factor to Bush firing him after the shellacking that the Republican party had in the [2006] midterms,” Eaton said. “All this sounds faintly familiar with what we’re going through right now. “But this is infinitely worse because we had a lot of other very smart people to corral the bad ideas coming out of Rumsfeld. [This time] we’ve had the whole removal of seasoned men and women who have learned things the hard way most of the time in combat. “If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is just evidence. The frustration is, we’re better than this in the uniformed military but we got handed a terrible set of guidance from our civilian leadership.” Michael O’Hanlon, a defense and strategy expert at the Brookings Institution, argued that the armed forces had enough “bench strength” to survive Hegseth’s purges without imminent collapse, but lamented the loss of certain key individuals who could not be easily replaced. He singled out Gen Chris Donahue, who recently stepped down from his post as head of the US land command in Europe and Africa. “We haven’t had a TV talkshow star with a strong partisan and cultural agenda wind up as secretary of defense,” said O’Hanlon. “There may be some echoes of previous secretaries, but the political and culture stuff is Pete Hegseth through and through.” Hegseth was “not going to wind up leaving a major mark”, O’Hanlon predicted. “He’s going to wind up being known as the guy who fought Trump’s culture wars for him – and maybe failed to help Trump stay out of trouble in the Iran war, depending on how bad that gets.” • This article was amended on 5 September 2026. An earlier version erred in saying that Robert McNamara became head of the International Monetary Fund; he was head (as its president from 1968 to 1981) of the World Bank, the IMF’s sister organization. • This article was amended on 6 September 2026 to include a statement from the Pentagon.

webTitle: Leftist insurgents are storming the midterms – just don’t call them all democratic socialists

fields.headline: Leftist insurgents are storming the midterms – just don’t call them all democratic socialists
fields.trailText: Progressive candidates navigate their ties to the DSA as the group faces historic growth and mounting pressure
fields.bodyText: Days before he won the Democratic primary for a US Senate seat in Michigan, insurgent newcomer Abdul El-Sayed was asked whether he was concerned about being labeled a “socialist”. “I’d rather think of myself as a capitalist who has actually read about capitalism,” El-Sayed told CBS News anchor Ed O’Keefe. “I’m not a socialist.” While El-Sayed might take pains to distance himself from the label in the swing state of Michigan, O’Keefe noted that the candidate has been linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the ascendant leftist group whose meteoric rise has captured the enthusiasm of voters desperate for bold change and whose recent wins have stoked the anxieties of both conservatives and the party’s establishment. “I’m not DSA,” El-Sayed stressed in the interview, though he made clear there is room for the DSA in the “big tent” he said he’s seeking to build. El-Sayed is just one of a number of progressive candidates and elected officials across the country who are navigating their relationship and differences with the DSA, which has come under increasing pressure as its candidates have won one race after the other in Democratic primaries mostly in blue states. But as other progressive candidates to the left of the Democratic establishment have mounted bids for office, there has at times been confusion about who is a “DSA candidate” – a confusion some Republicans have been eager to exploit. Some, like El-Sayed, espouse many of the group’s political priorities – fighting fascism, instating universal healthcare, getting money out of politics and boosting labor rights, to name a few – but are not members, nor have they been endorsed by the DSA. Others, like New York’s Claire Valdez, have been organizing with the group for years. Then there are those like Colorado’s Melat Kiros and Pennsylvania’s Chris Rabb who have long identified as socialists but only recently joined the organization. (All three are DSA-endorsed.) Brad Lander was once a member but left the group over its response to the 7 October 2023 attacks in Israel. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the national figure most often associated with the DSA, rejoined the New York City chapter last month after letting her membership lapse for seven years, as speculation mounts about her intention to run for president. But DSA membership doesn’t guarantee endorsement, and intense debates have roiled the organization in recent months about which candidates to endorse and how to best ride the current momentum. In Los Angeles, for example, the local DSA chapter voted to endorse mayoral candidate Nithya Raman this week after weeks of discussions on whether she was too centrist to earn their backing. Pragmatism v purism A decade into Trumpism and the Democrats’ failure to stop it, and buoyed up by the popularity of longtime member Zohran Mamdani, the DSA has helped popularize positions once viewed as radical – from taxing the rich to ending support for Israel. The DSA has become a “shorthand for this rebellion against Democratic party leadership”, said Peter Sterne, an editor at City & State New York who has extensively covered the DSA and a former member of the group. In recent months, the group has seen its membership soar to 120,000, its leaders are getting prime time on cable news and a recent poll found that one-third of Democrats now openly identify as “socialist”, a term not long ago viewed as a slur. The backlash has been swift. After DSA candidates won nine out of 10 races in which the group had fielded candidates in New York City in June, party establishment figures issued a string of hostile statements. Third Way, a centrist Democratic group, announced a $15m effort to go to “war” against them. DSA leaders and members have become tabloid fodder. And this week, House Republicans – joined by eight Democrats – adopted a resolution condemning “socialism” and specifically naming the DSA. The organization’s critics point to some of its more radical stances, from eliminating the Senate to abolishing borders and defunding the police, as a sign of its unseriousness. But many DSA members view those as aspirational and consistent with the group’s fundamental values, while calling for a more realistic approach. Even some more moderate Democrats recognize that the DSA’s message is resonating because the rest of the party has failed to present a satisfying vision of its own. “You can’t beat something with nothing,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington. “The more moderate wing of the Democratic party is going to have to raise its game substantially.” The DSA’s popularity and campaigning capacity on the one hand, and the animosity from more conservative corners on the other, has left some candidates, particularly in swing states, navigating a balancing act. In Florida, Angie Nixon, who recently won the Democratic Senate primary in one of the biggest upsets of the primary season, joined the DSA only in June but has not been endorsed by the group. When asked whether she identified as a democratic socialist, she equivocated. “I don’t agree with everything that they agree with, but they’re fighting hard to ensure we have access to universal healthcare, access to free college and fully funded public schools,” she said in an interview with the Guardian. “I’ve always been a lifelong Democrat but I’m more of [a] social democrat who believes in strong safety nets.” Some of the most popular politicians associated with the DSA have broken with the group on some issues. The group has for months been debating how to respond to a possible presidential run by Ocasio-Cortez. Some factions, and particularly many NYC-DSA members, have openly encouraged it, while others are suspicious of what they view as her willingness to compromise on DSA priorities. Mamdani has also broken with the group over policing. Ultimately, the decision will be made democratically – DSA members report often excruciatingly deliberative processes and stress that the “democratic” element of the group’s identity is just as fundamental as its socialist one. Endorsements, Sterne noted, can power a campaign with an “army” of canvassers and phone bank volunteers – the DSA’s New York City chapter says that its 50,000 volunteers knocked on doors 1.6m times in support of Mamdani’s candidacy. But the “DSA doesn’t just want to help get people into office and then let them do whatever they want”, he added, noting that there was some concern within the organization that candidates may opportunistically hitch their wagon to the group but not work with it after getting elected. The tension between the pragmatists and the purists, he argued, is healthy, and a sign of the organization’s strength. “More people are joining,” he said. “More people are identifying as socialists, which was once seen as a taboo term.”

webTitle: Trump downplays war with Iran, in which 18 US service members have been killed so far, as ‘small potatoes’ – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump downplays war with Iran, in which 18 US service members have been killed so far, as ‘small potatoes’ – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: The week ended with court rulings that were seen as wins for democratic elections in the country. A federal judge ruled that mail voting can continue for the midterms and Missouri’s supreme court denied a Republican-drawn congressional map meant to carve up a Democrat-held district. Donald Trump also, once again, downplayed the war in Iran, calling it “small potatoes” and threatened to axe trade with dozens of countries unless the Federal Reserve agreed to cut interest rates. Here’s what else happened today: Aiming to catch leakers, Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon subjected 50 members of the military’s Joint Staff to polygraph tests. According to the New York Times, the tests came after a deluge of leaks to the press about diminishing stock pile munitions. A federal judge extends block on Trump’s executive order, aimed at stifling mail voting. For a second time, a judge ruled that the presidents order to make a nationwide list of verified voters would result in “nearly guaranteeing significant disenfranchisement for eligible voters”. Despite 18 service members being killed so far in the Iran war, Trump called the conflict “small potatoes”. While speaking with reporters, the president minimized the war saying it wasn’t even a “war”, but rather a “military conflict”. He compared it to Vietnam and said it’s “not a big thing”. Trump signed an executive order geared toward supporting cattle ranchers, but also takes aim at delisting two species of wolves from the Endangered Species Act. The president said removing the gray wolf and Mexican wolf from the act would help ranchers “combat predation”. Missouri’s supreme court struck down a Republican-drawn congressional map that would’ve carved up a Democrat-held district. The ruling dealt a blow to Republican efforts to use redistricting to preserve their control of the House. John Fetterman is avoiding his work in the Senate, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal. A scathing report by the paper found that Fetterman, a democrat from Pennsylvania, whose views have increasingly diverged from those of his party, is frequently skipping constituent and committee meetings in lieu of appearances in conservative media. A report found that Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Trump’s former labor secretary, created a ‘toxic, intimidating and humiliating’ work environment. An investigation by the Department of Labor’s Office of Inspector General found that she had violated several department rules, including misusing public funds for travel, mistreating staff and carrying on an inappropriate relationship with a member of her security detail. Trump threatened to axe trade with dozens of countries unless the Federal Reserve agrees to cut interest rates. The President cited the strong August jobs report in a social media post pressuring his new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, to cut interest rates, a move Trump argues will juice the economy but that could also spark higher inflation. The US added an estimated 162,000 jobs in August, according to the Department of Labor. An unexpectedly strong August jobs report showed a rebound in hiring after a bleak summer for the labor market, with US firms adding jobs at a rapid clip despite economic headwinds downstream of the war in Iran. The American Civil Liberties Union hailed the federal judge’s ruling to block Donald Trump’s order that limited mail voting, calling it “critical protection” for elections. The group is joint-representing several plaintiffs in a lawsuit brought against the president. “States are already beginning to send mail ballots to voters for the November election, and this preliminary injunction provides a critical protection from the chaos that this rule would unleash,” the ACLU said in a statement with the plaintiffs and other counsel. US District Court Judge Indira Talwani initially placed a temporary order blocking Trump’s mandate and has now replaced that with a stronger preliminary injunction. Her injunction comes after Trump signed an executive order in March that would create a nationwide list of verified eligible voters and compel the US Postal Service to work with states to establish lists of mail-in voters before elections. This would mean a limited ballot delivery only to voters on those lists. A conjoined lawsuit was also brought by a coalition of 24 state attorneys general against the USPS. “As the court noted, mail ballots have been used since the Civil War,” the ACLU said in the joint statement. “Millions of citizens in the United States and overseas rely on mail ballots as a safe and trusted means of participating in our democracy.” Around 50 members of the military’s Joint Staff have been subject to polygraph tests, according to a report by the New York Times. The tests were reportedly part of the Pentagon’s goal to weed out personnel leaking sensitive information to the press. Some of the people required to take the polygraph tests were high-ranking officials, according to CBS News, including officials in Central Command and other combatant commanders. The polygraph tests reportedly came after several publications described diminishing stock pile munitions, such as Patriot interceptors and long-range missiles, in their reporting. Pete Hegseth, secretary of the Department of Defense, has sought to crackdown on leaks to the media. In July, he announced a joint task force to investigate leaks and identify those behind them. And as far back as March 2025, Hegseth warned that investigations into leakers would involve polygraph tests. The sheer number of people reported to have taken the tests is rare for the Pentagon, which uses polygraph tests but not in large swaths. “The Department does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters but takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly,” Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, said in an email. “Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world.” Donald Trump’s “Build the Wall” game is getting blowback from the game maker Tetris. The game, which is a near replica to the iconic falling blocks game, has the player build a structure to “protect the border from the coming horde.” In a post on X, Tetris wrote that: “we take copyright infringement very seriously.” The company added that it was not involved in the creation of the administration’s game and said, “at Tetris we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them”. The White House launched an “arcade” on Thursday, that houses five 80s-style computer games that includes “Build the Wall”. Other games involve the player flying a bald eagle down the National Mall and acting as border patrol agent along the Rio Grande river. Adam Telle said Friday that he is “honored” Donald Trump named him as the acting army secretary to replace Daniel Driscoll. He comes to the role, which is the army’s top civilian post, after serving as the assistant secretary of the army for civil works. “My previous work in the Army focused on moving at Trump Speed to deliver on one of the Army’s original missions,” Telle wrote in a post on X. “I will apply that same relentless focus on efficiency to how the Army mans, trains, equips, and modernizes.” Driscoll’s departure came after widespread reports of tensions with defense secretary Pete Hegseth. Driscoll gave no reason for leaving, but reportedly clashed with Hegseth after some of his allies had been ousted by Hegseth. Telle said Hegseth’s leadership at the department of defense is “historic” and that working closely with the department “we will deliver a more ready and capable Army”. On Truth Social, Trump called Telle: “A Great Patriot, who is respected by all.” Donald Trump’s executive order to limit mail-in voting has been blocked again by a federal judge. US District Court Judge Indira Talwani initially placed a temporary order blocking Trump’s mandate and has now replaced that with a stronger preliminary injunction. “Plaintiff States are required under state law to mail millions of ballots to voters on a prescribed timeframe. As detailed below, they are unable to pivot this late in the election cycle, nearly guaranteeing significant disenfranchisement for eligible voters,” the judge wrote in her ruling. Her injunction comes after Trump signed an executive order in March that would create a nationwide list of verified eligible voters and compel the US Postal Service (USPS) to work with states to establish lists of mail-in voters before elections. This would mean a limited ballot delivery only to voters on those lists. USPS has said in recent court filings that the technology needed to administer the order isn’t even available. Earlier this week, a USPS whistleblower came forward and warned of “potentially catastrophic problems” if the agency were to try and carry out the order. After Trump signed the order, a coalition of 24 state attorneys general joined together suing USPS to challenge the rule. They also filed a motion for the temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction as litigation was ongoing. Oral argument on the coalition’s request for a preliminary injunction was held on Thursday. “We’ve now secured longer-term relief that will keep the USPS changes blocked while our case moves forward,” said Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, which co-led the state coalition. “We will continue to take all steps to stop the Trump Administration from trampling on voting rights and restricting mail voting.” Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday that his real estate background has helped guide his knowledge on data centers. He said that if he were in charge of a city or state, he’d try to get in as many data centers as possible. “If you want your house to be more valuable and everything else, you’re going to want a data center,” Trump said. “If you want to go through poverty, crime, and squalor, I would say don’t approve data centers, you know, you have your choice.” The president’s remarks come as a nationwide backlash to data centers is underway, which is likely to be a flashpoint for the midterm elections. Town meetings have filled with constituents angry about massive data centers moving into residential neighborhoods and small towns. They worry about pollution, loud humming noise and strains on the electrical grid and water supply. The momentum has even caused some notable republicans, like Texas Governor Greg Abbot and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, to regulate data centers. While speaking with reporters on Friday, Trump said that he’s letting companies build their own power plants so they don’t have to use the grid, which would mean lower energy costs for residents. He didn’t mention, however, that would also mean excess pollution and smog for communities that would have the additional power plants in their backyards. “There’s a lot of places that want them, both in this country and in particular in China,” Trump said. The president is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s president, later this month. He told reporters that he’s looking forward to it. “He’s a great gentleman. We get along great. We have a very good trading relationship and you know they’re a competitor and all of that, but we have a very good relationship with President Xi,” Trump said. “He’s coming with his beautiful wife. She’s a beautiful woman and a great woman, respected all over the world.” Donald Trump minimized the war with Iran while speaking with reporters in the Oval Office on Friday. When asked how he would describe the conflict, if not a war, the president called it “small potatoes”. “A lot of people don’t call it a war. I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing,” Trump said. “We did Venezuela and we did this. In Venezuela we lost nobody. In this we lost 18 people and in Vietnam we lost 100,000 people and in other conflicts you lost tens of thousands of people.” When a reporter followed up, saying 18 service members have died and there are record-long deployments, Trump retorted: “Why is it record long? How long were we in Vietnam? How long were we in Vietnam? How long were we in Vietnam? We’re at five months now.” The war with Iran started in late February, nearly seven months ago. During the conflict, thousands of Iranians have been killed and more than 750 US service members have been wounded. The war has also brought soaring gas prices and disrupted food supply chains worldwide, as the blockade over the Strait of Hormuz has stifled trade and oil supply. Despite Trump saying Friday that the Iran war is not a “war”, he himself has repeatedly called it a war. Just on Monday, the president referred to it as “a relatively little war”. Trump told reporters Friday that “there’s no fighting right now”, despite a sharp escalation in the war this week with US strikes on Iran. He also said “we’re taking out a lot of oil” and “we control the Hormuz Strait”, both of these statements are not accurate. The president added that the US could hit Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, where nuclear facilities are reportedly housed, “very soon”. Democrats are raising concerns about the Department of Homeland Security deploying agents and law enforcement personnel to polling locations during the midterm elections. Members of the Committee on Homeland Security sent a letter to Markwayne Mullin, the DHS secretary, on Friday chastising him for brushing aside their requests for information on plans or policies for voting day. The committee wrote Mullin after he said earlier this week that he may send ICE agents to polling places “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down”. The letter states that DHS was established to defend the country against terrorist attacks, not disenfranchise eligible voters. It also says the deployment of armed men to polling facilities is illegal. “We sought your assurances that you would not deploy Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents,” the letter reads. “You ignored our letters.” Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday that he says is meant to support cattle ranchers. In it, he touted his voluntary “Product of USA” labeling, gaining access to millions of acres of land from the Department of the Interior and the US Forest Service and withdrawing from Biden-era environmental regulations. “The national herd is at a 75-year low, while consumer demand for beef has grown almost 10 percent over the past decade,” the order reads. Much of the executive order is geared toward “helping ranchers combat predation”. The administration is requesting that, within 90 days, the secretary of the interior look into whether it’s possible to delist the gray wolf and Mexican wolf from the Endangered Species Act. The order further says it will work with states to encourage them to also delist the two species of wolves and to “revise their standards for lethal takings”, which the administration says will help ranchers. Last week, Trump signed an order to temporarily increase imports of ‌some lower-tariff beef in an effort to bring down consumer beef prices, which have hit record highs this year. The president has been sharply criticized, including from members of his own party, since announcing the US will temporarily import up to 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef without charging higher tariffs. Four Democratic members of the House of Representatives are heading to Dallas to stump for the party ahead of the Republican National Committee’s 2026 midterm convention, which is set to take place in the city next week, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a statement Friday. The Democrats’ delegation includes Reps. Robert Garcia, Jason Crow, Madeleine Dean, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove. The four will partner with members of the Dallas area’s congressional delegation and the Texas Democratic Party, according to the statement. Texas, where the RNC is hosting its event, has only a few competitive House races this November. But it’s also the site of a close-run and consequential Senate race between Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, and James Talarico, a long-serving House Democrat. “While swing seat House Republicans try to hide from their record of raising costs on working families, gutting Medicaid to fund tax breaks for billionaire donors and supporting a reckless war of choice in Iran, House Democrats will be present to hold them accountable,” Jeffries said in the statement. The Missouri Supreme Court on Friday morning shot down a request from the state to delay an order to revert the state’s congressional districts to their earlier borders, before a Trump-backed redistricting effort by state Republicans. Missouri’s Secretary of State, Denny Hoskins, requested the delay in order to appeal the case to the US Supreme Court. The new map tossed out by the court was put into place by Missouri Republicans in 2025, and would’ve carved up a Democrat-held seat based around Kansas City. The court ruled that voters would need a chance to weigh in on the new Republican-drawn map before it could take effect, meaning it couldn’t be used for this year’s midterm election. The US added an estimated 162,000 jobs in August, according to the Department of Labor. An unexpectedly strong August jobs report showed a rebound in hiring after a bleak summer for the labor market, with US firms adding jobs at a rapid clip despite economic headwinds downstream of the war in Iran. It’s also a valuable economic win for the Trump administration ahead of the midterms, as Republicans seek to tamp down unease over inflation and soaring gas prices. Trump threatened to axe trade with dozens of countries unless the Federal Reserve agrees to cut interest rates. The President cited the strong August jobs report in a social media post pressuring his new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, to cut interest rates, a move Trump argues will juice the economy but that could also spark higher inflation. Should the central bank refuse, Trump said, he’d halt all trade between the US and nations with which it maintains a trade deficit — a long list of countries that includes the biggest US trading partners. A report found that Lori Chavez-DeRemer, Trump’s former labor secretary, created a ‘toxic, intimidating and humiliating’ work environment. An investigation by the Department of Labor’s Office of Inspector General found that she had violated several department rules, including misusing public funds for travel, mistreating staff and carrying on an inappropriate relationship with a member of her security detail. The report surfaced new details on the series of scandals that led to Chavez-DeRemer’s resignation back in April. John Fetterman is avoiding his work in the Senate, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal. A scathing report by the paper found that Fetterman, the Pennsylvania Democrat whose views have increasingly diverged from those of his party, is frequently skipping constituent appointments and committee meetings. Instead, he’s focused on advocating for the US alliance with Israel and appearing in conservative media, as he gains in popularity with Republican voters. Missouri’s supreme court struck down a Republican-drawn congressional map that would’ve carved up a Democrat-held district. The new map, backed by Trump, was gerrymandered to dismantle a congressional district currently held by Representative Emanuel Cleaver, a Democrat. The ruling, which held that voters would need to weigh in on the proposed changes, provoked outrage from Trump and Republican state lawmakers, and dealt a blow to Republican efforts to use redistricting to preserve their control of the House. The justice department on Friday indicted an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent for allegedly lying in an attempt to justify shooting a man in Minneapolis during an immigration crackdown earlier this year. According to the indictment unsealed Friday, Christian Castro, the ICE agent, had initially told investigators he shot a man in self-defense after multiple assailants tried to beat him with a shovel and a broom. In reality, according to the indictment, Castro had faced no such threat. Instead, he allegedly shot the wounded man, Julio Sosa-Celis, through the door of his residence as he fled from Castro. Before the shooting, Sosa-Celis allegedly rushed out of his residence to try to help extricate another man Castro was attempting to arrest, and who had fled on foot from a traffic stop. After a brief scuffle, the two men fled back inside the house, where the other man also lived. According to the indictment, the altercation that preceded the shooting had lasted roughly 11 seconds, not three minutes, as Castro first reported. It’s a rare case of Trump’s Justice Department charging an immigration officer in connection with a use of excessive force, after several such high-profile shootings have soured the public on his mass deportation campaign. Details of the indictment were previously reported by the Associated Press on Thursday. The outlet reported today that Mr Castro pleaded not guilty during his Friday hearing. Donald Trump is expected to sign an executive order related ⁠to beef today, ⁠sources told Reuters. One of the sources said ⁠the order would pertain to country-of-origin labeling for beef. Trump is scheduled to sign ⁠the executive order behind closed doors at 1.30pm ET, the outlet reported. Trump ‌said last week he would look into whether there were too many regulations restricting ranchers from slaughtering their own cattle. He also signed last week an order to temporarily increase imports of ‌some lower-tariff beef in an effort to bring down consumer beef prices, which have hit record highs this year. Trump has been sharply criticized, including from members of his own party, since announcing the US will temporarily import up to 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef without charging higher tariffs. Lori Chavez-DeRemer, who was Trump’s first pick to run the US Department of Labor before resigning in April amid a flurry of scandals, broke several of the agency’s rules during her chaotic tenure, the agency’s internal watchdog found in a report published yesterday. Chavez-DeRemer’s violations included – among other things – abusing public funds for personal travel, regularly drinking alcohol during work, and having “an inappropriately close and unprofessional relationship” with an agent on her protective detail, according to the report. She also had government workers carry out personal tasks for her and accepted gifts without reporting them through the official channels, the department’s office of inspector general found. The office noted that 38 witnesses described the environment created by Chavez-DeRemer and her top staff, as “toxic, intimidating and humiliating”. The report shed new light on the excesses of one of Trump’s lesser-known, but highly embattled, cabinet picks. Details of the investigation, including allegations of employee abuse, workplace drinking, and an affair between Chavez-DeRemer and a colleague, have been reported on since early this year. The US Department of Transportation opened an inquiry on Thursday into Tesla’s new CyberCab, the company’s latest take on a self-piloting robotaxi. The service debuted this week in Austin, Texas. Tesla’s founder, Elon Musk, billed it as “the future of transportation” in a post to social media. Just one problem, according to the Department of Transportation: Tesla informed regulators that the vehicles were compliant with the agency’s Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards. But the CyberCab lacks some crucial components, namely “conventional manual controls, such as a brake pedal, gas pedal, steering wheel, and mirrors,” which would typically be necessary to meet those criteria, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Now, the agency is reviewing how Tesla decided its vehicle met federal guidelines. “Among other things, NHTSA will consider the extent to which Tesla’s certification depended on determinations that certain FMVSS are inapplicable to the Cybercab,” the agency continued. President Trump threatened in a social media post on Friday to stop trade with some countries unless the US Federal Reserve moves to cut interest rates. Trump cited August’s strong jobs report as sufficient justification to lower rates, and warned that, if the central bank didn’t go along, he’d halt trade between the US and any nations with which it maintains a trade deficit. “LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post, aiming the appeal directly at his handpicked new Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh. “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change,” Trump wrote. The US runs a trade deficit – meaning it imports more goods from those nations than it exports to them – with dozens of countries, including some of its closest trading partners, among them Mexico, Canada and China. Trump has long tried to lean on the US central bank to lower interest rates, a move that, according to conventional monetary policy wisdom, can stimulate economic growth but risks worsening inflation. Despite Trump’s pleas, Warsh has hinted the Fed may instead raise interest rates to curb inflation, which remains well above its target of 2%. Warsh suggested the possibility of a rate hike during a speech at a summit in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, late last week. The Federal Reserve committee responsible for setting interest rate targets will meet on 15-16 September and announce whether the body will hike, maintain, or lower the current rate. The upcoming Labor Day weekend is set to be the most expensive on record for travelers paying at the pump, according to data from AAA. Americans will pay an average of about $4.15 for a gallon of gas this weekend – more than any other Labor Day weekend on record. At the same time, the price of diesel fuel has hit an all-time high of $5.85. Bringing down gas prices was a central promise of President Trump’s 2024 campaign, but that pledge has been undercut by the war in Iran and the closure of the strait of Hormuz, which has strangled energy markets. A Trump administration official told the Washington Post that President Trump is planning a trip to Ireland next week onboard his Qatari-gifted Air Force One – the same jet whose security vulnerabilities led Trump to secretly switch planes using a catering truck back in July. In Ireland, Trump reportedly plans to meet with Irish leaders and attend a golf tournament hosted at one of his golf clubs located in Doonbeg, Ireland, the Post reported on Friday. Trump had previously said that the aircraft’s security features would be beefed up before it returned to service. The scope of that work, as well as when, or if, it was fully completed, remains unclear. North Carolina is slated to begin sending out mail-in ballots today for November’s midterm elections, the first state to do so in spite of President Trump’s efforts to curtail voting by mail. More states are planning to follow North Carolina’s lead and start sending ballots in the coming weeks. As they do, the administration’s plan to overhaul mail-in voting may increasingly collide with the efforts of state elections officials trying to gear up for the midterms. Trump first issued an executive order in March seeking to impose new restrictions on voting by mail, mandating that states turn over voter data and only send ballots to a list of confirmed US citizens, to be compiled by the federal government. Under the plan, USPS could refuse to deliver ballots in states that didn’t go along. (Under the US constitution, states run their own elections, not the federal government.) Months of legal wrangling ensued. As things currently stand, a federal judge’s order has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from fully enforcing its new plan. The Trump administration has asked the supreme court to toss that order. The US Department of Labor dropped its August jobs report on Friday, and it was an unexpectedly strong showing for the US labor market, with American firms adding an estimated 162,000 new roles for the month. After a slow summer for hiring, the rosy August report will likely be a boon to the Trump administration. It arrives as Republicans, bracing for the midterms, seek to downplay the economic side effects of the escalating war in Iran, including creeping inflation, high gas prices, and turmoil in the bond market. According to the report, the added jobs have had little effect on the unemployment rate, which is holding at 4.1%. The report also revised up job growth estimates from the two previous months, including bumping July up from an estimated loss of 23,000 jobs to an increase of 21,000. More than three years into his Senate term, Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman has been frequently dodging work, as well as his own constituents, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday evening. Fetterman, a Democrat from Pennsylvania, was once a darling of his party, but has aligned himself more closely with Republicans since his 2022 election. Now, the Journal is reporting that Fetterman has forgone many of the duties of his office to focus on supporting Israel and making the rounds in conservative media. Fetterman has reportedly made a habit of denying or canceling meetings with constituents, including, in one case, bailing on a group of paralyzed veterans who’d arrived at his office. Not long after informing his staffers he wasn’t feeling well enough to take the meeting, Fetterman allegedly turned up at the office looking none the worse for wear, telling staff that he had an interview with Fox News he didn’t want to miss. In another notable incident, Fetterman reportedly declined to attend a funeral for three police officers killed near York, Pennsylvania, after learning the event would take three hours or longer. “This may be a nonstarter,” Fetterman reportedly told the staffer who informed him of the event’s expected duration. Russian state news agency Tass said the two US envoys ⁠seeking to end the war between Russia and Ukraine would visit both countries on Saturday and Sunday, but the Kremlin declined to comment. President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, last visited Moscow in January, when they held four hours of late-night talks with President Vladimir ⁠Putin in the Kremlin. “I wouldn’t make any announcements right now, but we will inform you when these contacts take place,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters when ⁠asked about the Tass report. A Missouri House race has been rocked by the Wednesday arrest of Republican candidate Thomas Ross, whom prosecutors accuse of attempting to frame his primary opponent Louise Secker for cocaine possession. In June, Ross allegedly gave his former campaign manager, identified by the initials “CS” in court documents, a bag of cocaine and Adderall. The two allegedly devised a plan for the former manager to stash the drugs in Secker’s purse or vehicle. On 21 June, prosecutors said, Ross asked for an update on the plot. “Taking it no luck with the substance of it all?” he wrote in a text to his staffer. “Substance” was a euphemism for the narcotics, authorities say. “I am actually creeping down to the car show right now and seeing if I can see your car. I have had it on me for a couple days in order to be able to take full advantage of any opportunity that arises,” the former manager replied, according to court documents. “I thought I had it at the forum Walter went to, but never got close [and] car was locked.” The Joplin police department in Missouri alerted the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on 30 July to a public corruption matter. It’s unclear how the police were alerted to the alleged scheme. The next day, the federal agency gave the former manager a covert recording device, which he used to tape a conversation with Ross. President Donald Trump said on Thursday he will ask Europeans to repay the American aid provided to Ukraine under the administration of his predecessor Joe Biden. Trump has long demanded that Europeans shoulder more of the cost of Western support for Ukraine in its war with Russia, which began more than four years ago. “Hundreds of Billions of Dollars was given to Ukraine and NATO, free of charge, that Europe would have paid for – If they were only asked, but we will be asking for that money, though somewhat belatedly!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Thursday. The president did not specify which countries he believed should pay. Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog. The Missouri supreme court blocked a Republican-drawn new congressional map ⁠from being used in November’s midterm ⁠elections, a blow to the party’s odds for maintaining its narrow US House majority. The ruling could save the House seat of longtime Democratic U.S. Representative Emanuel Cleaver. His Kansas City-based district had been dismantled under the redrawn map. “Despite the cynical and deeply shameful attempt to silence many of our neighbors, the people fought back and won,” Cleaver said in a social media post on Thursday. The decision marked a setback for Republicans in a national redistricting battle, AP reported, as Republicans had hoped Missouri’s new congressional boundaries could help them win an additional seat and hold on to their slim House majority in the midterms. “The referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely, and the secretary incorrectly concluded otherwise,” the court said in its ruling. The legislation containing the new districts “did not go into effect and will not go into effect unless and until approved by the voters.” As a result, the congressional map adopted after the 2020 census “remains in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election.” Missouri attorney general Catherine Hanaway, a Republican, said she would immediately appeal to the US supreme court, asserting that the decision “has thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis.” Meanwhile, Missouri governor Mike Kehoe, a Republican who backed the redrawn map, said on X: “We are extremely disappointed in today’s decision by unelected judges and their lack of respect for the legislative process.” Trump condemned the ruling in a post on Truth Social, saying it was “a Dark Day for ’Justice’ in Missouri!”. But Richard von Glahn, executive ⁠director of People Not Politicians, told reporters that “the Missouri constitution says what it says, and those words matter.” He added: “This is what democracy looks like. The people of Missouri demanded a voice, and the court just confirmed what we’ve been saying all along. People, not politicians, will have the final say.” In other developments: The Trump administration filed an emergency request asking the US supreme court to lift order blocking USPS from implementing mail-in voting restrictions. Chuck Schumer said the president was “[attempting] to destroy the integrity of our elections” with the move. Excavation work on Donald Trump’s “Great Triumphal Arch” project in Washington is set to begin in the coming weeks, interior secretary Doug Burgum said. Congressman Don Beyer, whose district includes Arlington National Cemetery, described the arch project as “illegal, gridlock-increasing [and] narcissistic”. Maryland’s supreme court has decided that a Democrat-backed congressional redistricting amendment can go before voters in the state in November in a win for Democrats. Donald Trump announced an interim replacement for army secretary, Dan Driscoll, who suddenly resigned earlier this week amid reports of tension between him and defense secretary Pete Hegseth. Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass has been asked to testify before a congressional subcommittee as part of an investigation into the “potential misallocation” of federal funds by the region’s Homeless Services Authority. Congressman Robert Garcia described the move as “another attempt by Donald Trump and House Republicans to launch a witch-hunt against Mayor Karen Bass and Los Angeles.”

webTitle: US judge extends block on Trump order to restrict mail-in voting

fields.headline: US judge extends block on Trump order to restrict mail-in voting
fields.trailText: Indira Talwani’s ruling presents major setback for president as first states begin to send out mail ballots for midterms
fields.bodyText: A federal judge on Friday again blocked Donald Trump’s executive order to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting, the latest in a legal back-and-forth playing out less than two months before election day. US district court judge Indira Talwani initially placed a temporary order blocking the president’s mandate and has now extended that prohibition with a stronger preliminary injunction. The ruling comes hours after North Carolina became the first state to start sending out mail-in ballots for the 3 November midterm elections. Talwani referred to the tight timeline in her ruling. “Plaintiff States are required under state law to mail millions of ballots to voters on a prescribed timeframe. As detailed below, they are unable to pivot this late in the election cycle, nearly guaranteeing significant disenfranchisement for eligible voters,” the judge wrote in her ruling. Trump signed an executive order in March that would create a nationwide list of verified eligible voters, compelling the US Postal Service (USPS) to work with states to establish lists of mail-in voters before elections. The result would mean a limited ballot delivery only to voters on those lists. The Trump administration had already appealed against her temporary block to the supreme court, and it appeared the justices were likely to have a final say on the matter. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the administration quickly appealed Friday’s ruling. The USPS has said in recent court filings that the technology needed to administer the order isn’t even available. Earlier this week, a USPS whistleblower came forward and warned of “potentially catastrophic problems” if the agency were to try to carry out the order. After Trump signed the order, a coalition of 24 state attorneys general sued the USPS to challenge the rule. They also filed a motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction as litigation was ongoing. Oral argument on the coalition’s request for a preliminary injunction was held on Thursday. “We’ve now secured longer-term relief that will keep the USPS changes blocked while our case moves forward,” said Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, who co-led the state coalition. “We will continue to take all steps to stop the Trump Administration from trampling on voting rights and restricting mail voting.” The order allows states to voluntarily use the new system. To date, not a single state has announced that it will do so. A coalition of voter service and civic groups, plaintiffs represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) in the lawsuit, issued a statement: “Today’s ruling makes it crystal clear: The US Postal Service must deliver all election mail. USPS has no authority in the Constitution or federal law over how states administer mail voting. And the President cannot order the Postal Service to create a disruptive new bureaucracy that will throw the election into chaos and disenfranchise untold numbers of voters.” Trump has long sought to limit mail voting, even though he himself often uses that method to cast his own ballot. He has falsely blamed mail balloting for his 2020 election loss, spreading baseless claims of fraud, but has so far been unable to change the longstanding voting procedure. An initial executive order Trump issued last year to change election rules, including a requirement for people to show documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote, was halted by federal judges. They ruled that the constitution gives states and, in some cases, Congress the power to set voting procedures, not the president. After Trump issued his mail voting executive order in March, Democrats and voting rights groups filed several lawsuits. Two ended up before Talwani, who placed an initial hold on the order in June, prohibiting its implementation until after November. But the supreme court late last month overturned that order. Its conservative majority pointedly did not say Trump’s move was legal but found the lawsuits were filed prematurely before the US Postal Service issued its rule on how it would implement the order. The rule came out just before the supreme court released its ruling, and the plaintiffs refiled their suits.
